title: Big Tech's AI Spending Binge Turns Cash Machines Into Cash Burners
excerpt: Alphabet's first-ever negative free cash flow and a fresh $25 billion bond sale signal a new era where the world's most profitable companies must borrow to fund the AI arms race.
body:
• Alphabet burned $5.9 billion in cash in Q2 2026 — its first negative free cash flow on record — even as Google Cloud revenue surged 82%.
  • The five largest hyperscalers are expected to spend over $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year, with aggregate free cash flow projected to turn negative at -$2.8 billion.
  • Alphabet raised $25 billion in a 10-tranche bond offering in early August, following Amazon's $25 billion bond sale in July, as debt becomes the primary funding mechanism for AI buildout.
  • The cost to insure Alphabet's debt against default reached its highest level in five years, signaling growing investor unease.

For years, Big Tech companies were celebrated as the world's most efficient cash machines — businesses so profitable they could fund enormous new bets while still showering shareholders with buybacks and dividends. The AI era has changed the math.

Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported its first negative free cash flow on record in the second quarter, burning through $5.9 billion even as its cloud computing unit posted a record 82% revenue increase, according to Reuters. The result sent Alphabet shares down roughly 6% and dragged other tech giants lower as investors recalibrated expectations for the entire sector.

The Scale of Spending

The numbers are staggering. Alphabet has raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to as much as $205 billion, up from an earlier cap of $190 billion, with another increase predicted for 2027. Together, the five major hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle — are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year on AI infrastructure, according to industry estimates.

Their aggregate free cash flow is projected to fall from $187 billion in 2025 to negative $2.8 billion in 2026, FactSet data show. By 2027, it could plunge to negative $41 billion.

"Investors will increasingly focus on how much of that cash must be reinvested simply to remain competitive — and whether AI revenue can grow faster than capital expenditure, depreciation and operating costs."

— Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist, Saxo Markets

Borrowing to Build

With internal cash flows no longer sufficient, Big Tech has turned to debt markets at an unprecedented pace. Alphabet filed a preliminary prospectus in early August for a $25 billion bond offering split across 10 tranches — just months after raising $20 billion in February as part of a multi-currency debt blitz, according to Barron's.

Amazon raised $25 billion in bonds in July. Together, the five big hyperscalers and AI entrant SpaceX are expected to issue $285 billion in bonds this year, up from about $109 billion last year, according to Barclays estimates.

The rising issuance has not gone unnoticed by credit markets. The cost of five-year credit default swaps on Alphabet's debt rose to 67.89 basis points on July 29 — the highest premium in at least five years, according to Barron's. While no one seriously doubts a top-rated company's ability to service its debt, the widening reflects growing hedging activity among banks and institutional investors.

The Profitability Squeeze

The capex-to-revenue ratio, a measure of how much of every sales dollar gets reinvested, is expected to nearly double across the group this fiscal year. Meta's ratio is projected to hit 54.9%, up from 35.9%. Alphabet's is set to reach 41%, up from 23%. Microsoft's is forecast at 45%, up from 31%, and Amazon's at 25%, up from 18%, according to Reuters.

Analysts expect Amazon to join Alphabet in burning cash in 2026, while Meta's free cash flow is projected to shrink 95.7% to just $1.85 billion. Microsoft fares best, though its expected $25.39 billion in cash is less than half the previous year's $58.74 billion.

Why They Keep Spending

Despite the financial strain, the competitive pressure is intense. Google Cloud's 82% growth rate is outpacing larger rivals, putting pressure on Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. Demand is so strong that Alphabet executives said they plan to rent out third-party data center capacity to serve clients, even at the cost of lower margins.

"Google Cloud was an absolute blowout," said Richard Clode, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors. "Alphabet has competitive advantage running all the way through the stack from their own custom AI chips through to distribution to billions of users."

For investors in the diaspora watching Silicon Valley's transformation, the shift raises a fundamental question: whether the AI buildout will generate returns fast enough to justify the borrowing — or whether the industry is building the most expensive infrastructure in history on the assumption that demand will catch up to supply.
